title: Ignatius on the road
hook: chained on his way to the lions, he writes that he is God's wheat (Romans 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement, and your line was let the proud be humbled. Did you give a little ground somewhere? Today, another letter headed for Rome, written in chains. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

A prisoner is being marched overland toward Rome, chained to a squad of soldiers. He calls them ten leopards, and says they only get worse when they're treated kindly. He is Ignatius, and in his letters he calls himself the bishop of Syria; tradition places his church in Antioch. He is going to Rome to die in the arena. Along the road, Christians come out to meet him in the towns he passes, and he writes letters to their churches. One letter goes ahead of him, to the Christians in Rome. It's a strange letter. It's a request. Please, don't save me.

Ignatius worries that the Roman Christians will try to step in. So he writes, in effect: say nothing on my behalf. Let me go. Then comes the picture that gives today its line. I am God's wheat, he writes, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. It's a startling thing to say about your own death. Wheat is not finished when it's harvested. It has to be ground before it can feed anyone. Some readers hear an echo of words Jesus says in John's Gospel: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." And for Christians who share bread at the Lord's table, the picture of becoming bread is hard to miss. Readers hear this letter in different ways. Some are moved by a man so sure of Christ that he walks toward the arena without flinching. Some are uneasy, and ask whether he wanted death too much. Both reactions take the letter seriously. And notice the rest of the road. A condemned man, with every reason to think only of himself, spends his last journey writing to other people's churches: be united, gather together often, care for the widows, be patient with one another. He is already being ground into bread, letter by letter, for people he would never see again.

Here's the practice: think of your life as bread for others. Settle, and breathe. Bread is ordinary. It gets broken, shared, eaten, gone. Bring to mind the people who are fed, in some way, by your days: the ones you cook for, work for, listen to, look after. Picture each one for a breath. Then ask: what in me is being ground down right now, and could it become something that feeds someone? Tiredness, patience, time. If you pray, you can offer your day to God as bread. If you don't, simply hold the people who depend on you. The bell holds the time.
Ignatius. A bishop chained on the way to Rome, writing to churches as he goes, and asking the Romans to let him become God's wheat.
Your line: god's wheat. Today, at the moment you feel ground down, do one small thing that feeds someone else. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches remember Ignatius of Antioch as a saint and martyr, and his letters are read today among the writings of the Apostolic Fathers.

fork.setup: you're a Christian in Rome with friends in high places. Ignatius is being marched to the arena. what do you do?

do what he asks: don't interfere.
fork.reveal: he begs the Romans not to save him: he is God's wheat, to be ground into pure bread of Christ.

original.note: Greek: I am God's wheat (Ignatius, to the Romans 4).

trapdoor: what you thought: an early Christian who wanted to die.
what it means: a prisoner who refused rescue, and spent his last road writing to other people's churches.
what a scholar hears: wheat ground into pure bread, echoing John 12:24 and the bread of the Lord's table; readers still argue over his eagerness.
recall: waiting for the consolation of Israel

notes: Editor pass: speculation about Roman 'friends with influence' cut; the John 12:24 link now attributed to 'some readers'; 'ever since' cut from the trapdoor; stray blank line in notes removed.

Ignatius is paraphrased throughout (Lightfoot's translation not verified word for word): 'ten leopards' who grow worse when treated kindly (Romans 5); 'bishop of Syria' (Romans 2); his request that the Romans not intervene (Romans 1–2, 4); 'I am God's wheat... pure bread of Christ' (Romans 4). Check each.
'Tradition places his church in Antioch': Eusebius and later tradition; confirm.
The bread/Eucharist echo is offered as 'hard to miss' for Christians who share bread at the Lord's table; churches understand the Eucharist differently, and the script does not take a side.
The summary of his advice ('be united, gather together often, care for the widows, be patient with one another') draws from To the Ephesians 13 and To Polycarp 1, 4; confirm.
Original: σῖτός εἰμι θεοῦ (Romans 4). Confirm accents.
